📌 Governance Snapshots: Why Your Tokens May Not Count in a DAO Vote

Main Points
⏺ Some DAOs calculate voting power using token balances from a specific blockchain block
⏺ Buying tokens after that snapshot may not increase your voting power
⏺ This post explains how balance snapshots work and why purchase timing matters

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol records balances at a selected block to determine how many votes each participant receives.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — a fixed reference point prevents voting power from changing every time tokens are transferred during the voting process.
3️⃣ Example — a vote uses balances from block #1000, but you buy tokens at block #1005. Those new tokens won't increase your voting power for that proposal.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — users may buy governance tokens specifically to participate, only to discover the snapshot already happened.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before buying governance tokens, check the snapshot block, delegation conditions, and voting eligibility rules.

Final Thoughts

DAO governance isn't only about how many tokens you hold. It can also depend on when you held them. Sometimes your voting power is decided before the vote even begins.

No Holds Barred: Trump Leads GOP’s All-Out Attack on Democrats


With the 2026 midterm elections approaching their final stretch, Republicans are increasingly relying on a familiar political weapon: personal attacks against their Democratic opponents. 

Led by Trump, the party has shifted its closing campaign message toward a barrage of accusations, provocative claims and political character assaults. The strategy comes at a difficult moment for the GOP. Voter frustration over inflation, the cost of living and dissatisfaction with the president is creating serious challenges for Republican candidates. 

Rather than focusing exclusively on their economic record or presenting a clear legislative agenda, party leaders have increasingly turned their attention to discrediting Democrats. 

Trump has been at the center of this approach, using his enormous political platform to amplify attacks against Democratic candidates. The accusations have become increasingly aggressive, with some claims lacking credible factual support.

For Republicans, the calculation is straightforward: energize their political base, dominate the news cycle and shift public attention away from issues that could hurt the party at the ballot box. 

Personal controversies can generate headlines far more quickly than detailed discussions about economic policy or government performance.But the strategy also carries risks. 

Negative campaigning may mobilize loyal supporters, yet it can alienate independent voters and Americans who are increasingly exhausted by the constant hostility in Washington. 

For voters worried about grocery bills, housing costs and financial security, another round of political name-calling offers little reassurance that their everyday problems will be addressed. The increasingly personal nature of the campaign also reflects a broader transformation within the Republican Party. 

Under Trump, political confrontation has become a defining feature of the party's public identity. Candidates are operating in an environment where loyalty, aggressive messaging and the ability to dominate the media conversation often compete with traditional policy debates. 

The Democrats, meanwhile, have an opportunity to turn the Republican strategy into a liability by keeping the focus on the economy, voters' concerns and the credibility of their opponents' claims.

As Election Day approaches, the central question is whether Trump's confrontational approach will succeed in rallying Republican voters or deepen the frustration of Americans who want political leaders to address the country's problems rather than wage another round of personal battles. 

One thing is increasingly clear: the final days of the 2026 midterm campaign are becoming less about competing visions for America's future and more about the politics of accusation, confrontation and personal attacks.

👀 Justin Sun becomes PEPE’s largest individual holder, Arkham says 

🌐 Tron founder Justin Sun has accumulated nearly 3% of PEPE’s supply, with blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence identifying approximately $51.25 million worth of the memecoin across his known and suspected wallets. According to an October 27 Arkham Intelligence report, the tokens entered Sun-linked wallets over the previous 10 days, making him the largest individual PEPE holder outside cryptocurrency exchanges.

🔗 The firm estimated his combined holdings at 2.82% of PEPE’s supply, although some wallets included in its calculations were attributed to Sun through blockchain analysis. At the time, PEPE had a market capitalization of approximately $1.81 billion, with exchanges controlling several of the largest known holdings.

📊 Binance held $337.5 million worth of PEPE, representing 18.7% of the supply, followed by Robinhood with $150.9 million, or 8.37%. Coinbase and OKX accounted for another 5.03% and 4.15%, respectively. Unlike Sun’s attributed holdings, exchange balances generally include assets held on behalf of customers, meaning their large positions do not necessarily represent investments made by the platforms themselves.
